nameStory: Woolly burdock gets its name from the dense, soft hairs that cover its leaves and stems, giving them a fuzzy, wool-like texture. The word 'burdock' comes from 'bur' (referring to the prickly seed heads that stick to everything) and 'dock' (an old term for large-leaved plants). Run your fingers along a leaf and you'll immediately understand why early botanists chose 'woolly' to describe this particularly fuzzy member of the burdock family.
description: Woolly burdock is a robust biennial plant that can grow 3-6 feet tall, forming large rosettes of heart-shaped leaves in its first year before sending up flowering stems in its second year. The entire plant has a distinctly fuzzy appearance due to dense, white hairs covering the leaves and stems. Like its burdock relatives, it produces purple thistle-like flowers followed by the infamous bur-covered seed heads that hitchhike on clothing and animal fur. This European native is much less common in New England than its two cousins, greater and lesser burdock.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large heart-shaped leaves covered in dense white woolly hairs, especially on the undersides, giving them a soft, flannel-like texture when touched

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple thistle-like flower heads about 1 inch across, clustered at branch tips, blooming from summer into fall

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms large rosettes of leaves in first year, then sends up branching flower stalks 3-6 feet tall in second year before dying

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round burs covered in hooked spines that grab onto clothing and fur with remarkable tenacity, containing dark seeds inside

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, grooved stems densely covered in white woolly hairs that feel soft to the touch, unlike the smoother stems of other burdocks

habitat: Woolly burdock grows in disturbed soils along roadsides, field edges, and waste places, preferring full sun to partial shade. It thrives in rich, moist soils but can tolerate various soil types as long as they're not waterlogged. In New England, it's quite rare compared to its relatives, most often found in areas with recent soil disturbance.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants emerge as rosettes of fuzzy heart-shaped leaves close to the ground, with the woolly texture already apparent on young foliage.
seasonality.summer: Second-year plants send up tall flower stalks topped with clusters of purple thistle-like blooms that attract bees and butterflies throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Flowers mature into the characteristic burs that cling to anything that brushes against them, while lower leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stalks persist with dried burs still attached, continuing to disperse seeds, while first-year rosettes may remain green under snow.

funFact: The tiny hooks on burdock burs inspired the invention of Velcro in 1941 when Swiss engineer George de Mestral examined them under a microscope after picking them off his dog's fur during a hunting trip.
confusionNotes: Woolly burdock is easily distinguished from its common relatives by its distinctly fuzzy, white-haired leaves and stems - if it feels soft and woolly to the touch, you've found the right species. Greater and lesser burdock have much smoother, less hairy foliage that feels rougher when touched.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being the rarest burdock in New England with only one recorded observation, woolly burdock is actually quite common in parts of Europe and Asia. Like other burdocks, its roots are edible when young and are used in traditional herbal medicine, though proper identification is essential before any use.
compareHints: Woolly burdock stands out from greater burdock and lesser burdock primarily by its dense white woolly covering that gives leaves and stems a soft, flannel-like texture. While all three species produce similar purple flowers and sticky burs, only woolly burdock maintains that distinctly fuzzy appearance throughout its growth. The other two species have much smoother, less hairy surfaces that feel rougher to the touch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Lesser burdock is smaller overall than greater burdock and has shorter leaf stalks, making the heart-shaped leaves appear to sit closer to the stem.
Greater burdock is significantly larger than lesser burdock in all aspects - bigger leaves, taller stems, and larger burrs.
